Munich’s Marienplatz is framed by the elaborate stone New Town Hall, with pointed turrets and a central clock tower. Nearby, the Frauenkirche’s two rounded tower caps rise above lower rooftops. Pedestrian streets have pale facades, German shop signs and orderly café seating; blue trams and suburban trains serve the wider centre. Footsteps on paving, bicycle bells and conversations mix with tram and train sounds. Summer sun makes the stone glow, while winter brings low light and heavy coats. Residents and visitors wear everyday city clothes, with some traditional Bavarian dress visible at festivals. A local greeting is “Grüß Gott” or the informal “Servus.”

Hamburg’s harbour spreads along the broad, tidal Elbe. Container cranes stand above stacked steel boxes and long ships; near the waterfront, the Elbphilharmonie’s rippling glass top rises from a red-brick base. Speicherstadt’s brick warehouses and narrow canals lie close by. At the Landungsbrücken piers, ferries rock gently, then pull away leaving foamy wakes. German signs mark terminals and quays. Gulls call over engine rumble, ferry horns and water slapping against pilings. The light is often cool under moving cloud, with wind lifting coats and hair. Dock workers, commuters and visitors wear practical layers and may greet one another with “Moin.”

Amsterdam’s center has narrow brick canal houses, often four or five stories tall, with steep gables, tall windows and occasional hoisting beams above the top floor. Dark canal water reflects stone bridges, moored boats and rows of trees. Bicycles pass in steady streams along marked lanes, their bells ringing as riders slow for pedestrians; trams rumble and squeal around bends. Dutch-language signs hang above ground-floor shops and cafés. Overcast light makes the brick look deep red-brown, while low sun glints off windows. People wear practical coats or rain jackets and greet one another with “hoi” or “goedemorgen.”

Brussels Grand Place is a broad paved square enclosed by closely packed, ornate guildhall façades with gilded details, sculpted stonework and steep roofs. The taller Gothic Town Hall has a slender, pointed tower that rises well above the surrounding buildings. Café tables occupy parts of the square; visitors walk across uneven stone paving and pause to photograph the façades. French and Dutch appear on nearby signs and menus. Warm evening lighting picks out gold trim against gray stone, while cloudy daylight flattens the colors. Footsteps, conversation and occasional church bells carry across the open space. People in coats or casual travel clothes say “bonjour” or “goedendag.”

Montmartre climbs through narrow Paris streets and long flights of stone steps toward the white domes of Sacré-Cœur. Cream and pale-gray buildings have wrought-iron balconies, mansard roofs and small street-level cafés with French signs. Around Place du Tertre, artists set easels beside closely spaced restaurant terraces. Pedestrians climb at uneven speeds, and a funicular carries passengers up the steep slope. On clear days, the hill overlooks a dense spread of gray Paris rooftops; in damp weather, the paving darkens and reflects shop lights. Expect footsteps, café chatter and distant traffic rather than constant music. Locals wear everyday urban clothes and greet shopkeepers with “bonjour.”

The Champs-Élysées is a long, broad avenue with several lanes of moving cars, wide pavements and double rows of clipped trees. Looking uphill, the pale stone Arc de Triomphe anchors the far end; looking downhill, the avenue opens toward Place de la Concorde. Large shop windows, café terraces and French-language signs line the pavements. Traffic surges and pauses at lights, with engine noise beneath footsteps and overlapping conversation. Summer sunlight falls through the trees in broken patches; after rain, headlights stretch across the wet roadway. Shoppers, commuters and tourists wear varied city clothes. A typical greeting inside a shop is “bonjour.”

Nice’s seafront curves along the Baie des Anges, with a broad paved promenade, palm trees, pebble beaches and blue-green Mediterranean water. Pale cream and ochre apartment façades face the coast; farther along the Riviera, built-up bays alternate with rocky headlands and crowded marinas. Waves rattle the beach pebbles as they retreat. Bicycles and walkers move along the promenade, while cars pass steadily behind it. Strong sun gives the sea a bright turquoise edge, though wind can make the water choppy. French signs dominate, with Italian visible in some restaurants. People wear light summer clothes or jackets in cooler months and greet others with “bonjour.”

Lyon sits between the Rhône and Saône rivers, crossed by bridges carrying cars, cyclists and pedestrians. In Vieux Lyon, narrow cobbled lanes run between warm ochre and pink Renaissance façades with shuttered windows; elsewhere, broader streets have pale stone apartment blocks and French shop signs. The white Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière stands high above the old town. River water moves slowly beneath the bridges, catching bands of evening light. Footsteps echo in older passages, while buses, trams and conversation fill busier streets. Weather shifts from bright, warm afternoons to gray, damp days. People wear ordinary city clothes and greet one another with “bonjour.”

Around Westminster, the Elizabeth Tower’s clock face rises above the Gothic stone of the Palace of Westminster beside the Thames. Westminster Abbey has pointed arches and twin west towers; nearby roads carry red double-decker buses, black cabs, cyclists and pedestrians. Stone façades range from pale cream to weathered gray, with English street signs and bus-stop boards. Traffic crawls and accelerates in short bursts, buses hiss at stops, and bells may sound above river and road noise. London light is often soft under cloud, with brief sharp reflections after rain. Office workers, visitors and officials wear anything from suits to raincoats; greetings include “hello” and “morning.”

Camden’s main streets mix brick shopfronts, large colorful storefront signs and dense crowds around the markets. Along the Regent’s Canal, narrowboats sit low in dark water beside towpaths, iron bridges and old brick warehouse buildings. Market passages contain small clothing stalls, food counters and English-language signs, sometimes with other languages on menus. People weave around one another at walking pace; buses brake on Camden High Street while market voices, buskers and traffic overlap. Cloudy daylight leaves brick and painted metal subdued, but shop lights brighten the covered stalls. Visitors and locals wear everything from office clothes to bold alternative fashion; a casual greeting is “hello” or “alright?”

Manchester’s centre mixes dark red-brick warehouses with pale stone civic buildings and glass office towers. The Manchester Town Hall’s clock tower rises above Albert Square, while canals cut between former mills in nearby districts. Streets are often damp beneath a low grey sky, making tram tracks and brickwork shine. Yellow-and-silver Metrolink trams glide through the centre with a soft motor whine and warning bell; buses and delivery vans add a steady rumble. English shop signs, football shirts, coats and trainers are common. Around cafés and tram stops, people greet each other with “Hiya” or “You alright?”

Edinburgh Castle sits on a dark volcanic rock above the Old Town’s tightly packed grey-brown stone buildings. The Royal Mile slopes over uneven paving between narrow closes; across the valley, the New Town has orderly pale sandstone terraces and broad streets. Wind moves through the lanes, and changing cloud cover shifts the stone from warm beige to charcoal within minutes. Buses hiss at stops, footsteps strike stone, and bagpipes may be heard near busy visitor spots. English signs dominate. People wear practical coats and scarves much of the year, greeting acquaintances with “Hiya” or “You alright?”

The River Liffey divides central Dublin, crossed by low bridges including the white, arched Ha’penny Bridge. Georgian streets show rows of red-brown brick houses with tall sash windows and brightly painted front doors; commercial streets mix older stone fronts with modern glass. Cloudy daylight and brief rain showers leave the pavements reflective. Green-and-silver Luas trams roll past with a bell, alongside buses, bicycles and lively conversation outside pubs. Signs are commonly in English, with Irish on public signs and transport. People in jackets and everyday work clothes greet each other with “Howya?” or “Hiya.”

Madrid’s Gran Vía is a broad avenue lined with ornate early twentieth-century stone façades, projecting balconies, domes and modern shopfronts. The dark dome and gilded figure of the Metrópolis Building mark its eastern end; near Callao, tall signs and illuminated screens rise above crowds. Strong sun throws sharp shadows across pale façades, while evening brings bright storefront light. Cars, taxis and buses flow between marked crossings, with engines, horns and footsteps echoing off the buildings. Signs are mainly in Spanish. Shoppers and office workers wear contemporary city clothes and often greet someone with “Hola” or “Buenas.”

Barcelona’s Gothic Quarter is a web of narrow pedestrian lanes between weathered beige stone buildings. Shuttered windows, iron balconies, small squares and the soaring stone façade of Barcelona Cathedral appear around sudden corners. Direct sun reaches the wider plazas, but many lanes stay shaded even at midday. Footsteps echo on paving stones; café voices, rolling suitcase wheels and an occasional delivery cart carry through the passages. Scooters and buses are heard mainly along the surrounding roads. Signs often appear in Catalan as well as Spanish. Locals and visitors wear casual clothes, greeting people with “Bon dia” or “Hola.”

Seville has pale stucco walls, wrought-iron balconies, colourful ceramic tiles and orange trees along its streets and squares. The Giralda bell tower rises above the cathedral, while the narrow lanes of Santa Cruz open into small, shaded courtyards. Summer sunlight is intense, making white walls glow and casting crisp shadows beneath awnings; people seek shade or gather outside later in the evening. Footsteps, café conversation, scooters and occasional church bells fill the air. A horse-drawn carriage may pass near the cathedral with measured hoofbeats. Signs are in Spanish. People dress lightly in hot weather and greet others with “Hola” or “Buenas.”

Lisbon’s historic trams are compact, usually yellow cars with rounded fronts, cream roofs, large windows and narrow interiors. Tram 28 winds slowly through steep, tight streets beside tiled façades and worn stone pavements. Its wheels follow steel rails set into the road; on bends they squeal, and the body rocks gently as it climbs or descends. A trolley pole touches the overhead wire, while the motor hums and a sharp bell warns pedestrians. Bright sun can flash across windows before the tram enters deep street shade. Stop signs are in Portuguese; passengers commonly say “Bom dia” or “Olá.”

Porto climbs steeply above the Douro River. Along the Ribeira waterfront, narrow houses in ochre, cream and faded red stand close together beneath red tile roofs; blue-and-white azulejo tiles cover many walls elsewhere. The two-level iron Dom Luís I Bridge spans the river, with metro trains crossing its upper deck. Streets shift between cobblestones and smoother paving, and low sun picks out the uneven façades. Riverfront voices, gulls, traffic and the soft rumble of trains overlap. Portuguese shop signs hang above cafés and small stores. People in casual jackets and walking shoes greet each other with “Olá” or “Bom dia.”

Trastevere has narrow, uneven streets paved with dark sampietrini cobbles, ochre and terracotta stucco buildings, green shutters, and ivy climbing around doorways. Small cars and scooters ease around pedestrians; wheels rattle sharply over the stones. In Piazza di Santa Maria, a fountain faces the church’s broad facade, while outdoor tables fill the edges. Warm evening light catches worn plaster and hanging signs in Italian. Expect conversation, clinking glasses, church bells, and scooter engines rather than constant heavy traffic. Residents in everyday city clothes pass visitors with cameras; greetings include “buongiorno” during the day and “ciao” between acquaintances.

Piazza del Duomo is a broad stone-paved square dominated by Milan Cathedral’s pale marble facade, crowded with pointed spires and statues. The arched entrance to Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II opens off the square, revealing iron-and-glass roofing and mosaic floors. Trams, including older yellow cars, move along nearby streets with a metallic rumble and bell; footsteps, voices, and pigeons fill the open space. Sunlight makes the marble nearly white, while overcast skies bring out its gray veining. Commuters in coats or business clothes cross among visitors taking photographs. Shop signs are mainly Italian; people greet one another with “buongiorno” or “ciao.”

Florence’s center has tight stone streets opening onto piazzas framed by cream and ochre buildings with green shutters. The cathedral’s patterned white, green, and pink marble and huge red-tiled dome rise above the roofs; the Arno passes beneath Ponte Vecchio’s shop-lined span. Sun warms the pale facades and casts deep shadows across narrow lanes. Footsteps echo on paving stones, bicycle bells ring, and scooters buzz through streets where vehicles are permitted; church bells carry over the squares. Street signs and menus are in Italian. Locals in ordinary city clothes walk beside visitors, greeting shopkeepers with “buongiorno” and friends with “ciao.”

Naples stacks dense cream, peach, and weathered gray buildings against steep streets above its bay; on clear days, Vesuvius forms a broad, low silhouette across the water. In the older center, narrow lanes run between tall facades with balconies, shutters, laundry, and ground-floor food shops. Scooters thread carefully through pedestrians, their engines mixing with calls from shopfronts, traffic horns, and church bells. Bright sun hits the upper walls while the lanes stay shaded; sea air and haze soften distant views. Signs are in Italian. People wear everyday city clothes, and greetings include “buongiorno,” “ciao,” and the Neapolitan “uè” between acquaintances.

Plaka climbs the slopes beneath the Acropolis through narrow stone lanes and steps. Low neoclassical houses have pale yellow, cream, or pink plaster, shuttered windows, balconies, and flowering vines; higher up, Anafiotika’s small whitewashed houses sit close together. The Acropolis walls and columns appear above the roofs. Hard summer sunlight leaves crisp shadows, while outdoor tables occupy shaded corners. Footsteps, conversation, dishes, and occasional distant traffic are more prominent than engines in the pedestrian lanes. Greek lettering appears on street signs, often alongside English on menus. Residents and visitors dress casually; local greetings include “kaliméra” in the morning and “yássas” when addressing someone politely.

Mykonos town is a maze of low, whitewashed cubic buildings with blue, green, or red wooden doors and shutters. Its narrow stone walkways are traced with white-painted joints; near the waterfront, Little Venice’s balconies project toward the sea, and the Kato Mili windmills stand on a bare ridge. Strong sun creates brilliant white walls and hard blue shadows. Wind moves awnings and loose clothing, while waves slap the harbor edge and boats hum beyond it; footsteps and conversation fill the lanes. Signs mix Greek and English. Visitors in light summer clothes pass local workers, who may greet them with “kaliméra” or “yássas.”

Zurich’s old town lines both sides of the Limmat with narrow lanes, painted and stone facades, steep roofs, and church towers; Grossmünster’s twin towers are a clear landmark. Along larger streets, blue-and-white trams glide on rails with a soft whine and bell, while people walk or cycle beside the river. Lake Zürich opens beyond the center, reflecting pale winter light or bright summer skies. Shop signs are mainly German, with other languages visible around the station. People wear practical city clothes, often coats in colder months. Footsteps, tram bells, and riverside conversation accompany greetings such as the Swiss German “grüezi” and familiar “hoi.”

At Geneva’s lakeside, broad quays, stone embankments, trees, and flower beds frame blue-gray water dotted with swans and boats. The Jet d’Eau sends a tall white plume upward when operating; wind bends its spray and can wet the nearby walkway. Paddle steamers and smaller ferries cross the lake, their engines and horns audible beneath conversation and the soft slap of water against the shore. Clear weather reveals mountains beyond the far end; cloud or mist can hide them. French dominates signs and announcements. Commuters, walkers, and visitors share the quays, greeting others with “bonjour” or, among friends, “salut.”

Stockholm spreads across islands, with pale stone waterfront buildings, copper-green roofs and bridges crossing dark blue water. Gamla Stan has narrow cobbled lanes, ochre and rust-coloured façades, while the brick City Hall rises beside a broad quay. Signs are mainly in Swedish. Buses, blue-and-white ferries, cyclists and pedestrians move steadily; ferry wakes slap against the stone edges, and trams hum past their stops. Summer light lingers into the evening; winter daylight is brief, with wet pavement or snow reflecting streetlamps. People wear practical coats and scarves in cold weather and greet each other with “hej” or “god morgon.”

Oslo sits between wooded hills and a harbour lined with ferries, cranes and newer glass-and-stone buildings. The white marble Opera House slopes down to the water, and trams pass older plaster and brick blocks farther inland. Shop and street signs are mostly Norwegian. Electric buses, bicycles and cars move through broad, orderly streets; listen for tram bells, tyres on damp asphalt and gulls near the quay. Summer evenings are bright, while winter brings low sun, snow or icy patches. People wear rain jackets or insulated coats according to season and commonly greet each other with “hei” or “god morgen.”

Nyhavn is a short Copenhagen canal bordered by narrow, tightly packed houses painted mustard yellow, orange, red and blue, with steep roofs and café tables along the cobbled quays. Wooden boats and low canal-tour vessels sit beneath dense lines of masts and rigging. Danish signs hang from ground-floor restaurants; bicycles are parked in clusters nearby. Boats advance slowly, pushing small ripples against the quay, while footsteps, conversation, bicycle bells and gulls carry across the water. Sunlight catches the bright façades, though cloud and rain can turn the canal grey. Visitors mingle with locals in casual layers; a usual greeting is “hej.”

Helsinki has broad streets, pale neoclassical façades and blocks of granite, brick and modern glass. The white Helsinki Cathedral rises above Senate Square; near the harbour, market stalls face ferries and open water. Signs are chiefly Finnish and Swedish. Blue-green trams glide around bends with a rail squeal, while gulls call over the waterfront and tyres hiss on wet streets. Summer light lasts late; winter is dim, with snowbanks and a low sun. People wear dark coats, boots and hats in the cold, lighter layers in summer, and greet one another with “moi” or “hei.”

Reykjavik’s centre is low-rise, with colourful houses clad in painted corrugated metal beside concrete shops and cafés. Hallgrímskirkja’s stepped grey tower stands above the streets; the faceted glass Harpa concert hall faces the harbour. Signs are mostly Icelandic, with English common around visitor businesses. Cars pass on compact roads, and pedestrians lean into sudden gusts. Wind rattles signs and coats, gulls cry near the water, and tyres swish over rain-dark asphalt. The light changes quickly between sun and cloud; winter days are short. People dress in waterproof layers and sturdy shoes, greeting others with “hæ” or “góðan dag.”

Brooklyn varies by neighbourhood: rows of brick and brownstone stoops line residential blocks, while DUMBO has converted brick warehouses, cobbles and views toward the Manhattan and Brooklyn bridges. Taller apartment towers cluster near parts of the waterfront. Signs are mainly English, with Arabic storefront lettering on Atlantic Avenue and other languages across the borough. Yellow taxis, delivery bikes, buses and pedestrians share busy crossings; subway trains rumble overhead on elevated stretches. Light bounces between buildings, and summer pavement shimmers with heat. Residents dress in everything from office clothes to casual streetwear and greet acquaintances with “hey” or “how you doing?”

Central Park is a long green space framed by Manhattan apartment towers. Curving asphalt paths cross lawns and wooded slopes; stone arches, the tiled Bethesda Terrace and the slender Bow Bridge provide recognisable landmarks. Signs are in English, and park maps stand near entrances. Joggers pass at a steady pace, cyclists follow marked drives, and rowboats drift slowly across the lake. Footsteps, birdsong, bicycle bells and distant traffic overlap; fountains add a steady splash near Bethesda Terrace. Summer trees cast dense shade, autumn leaves turn orange, and winter can leave bare branches over snow. Visitors and locals wear seasonal casual clothes and say “hi” or “good morning.”

Hollywood Boulevard has low and mid-rise shops, theatres and hotels, with star-shaped plaques set into the dark sidewalk. The ornate TCL Chinese Theatre and the Hollywood and Highland shopping complex draw crowds; the white Hollywood Sign sits far away on a hillside, visible only from suitable viewpoints. Storefront signs are mostly English, with Spanish also common. Cars and buses roll through wide intersections as pedestrians stop for photos; engines, conversations and crossing signals fill the air. Strong sun casts sharp palm-tree shadows, while evenings glow with marquees and headlights. Clothing ranges from casual T-shirts to workwear, and greetings include “hey,” “how’s it going?” and “hola.”

Santa Monica meets the Pacific at a broad pale-sand beach below low bluffs. The pier projects over moving green-blue water, with its Ferris wheel, timber decking, railings and small rides visible from the shore. Downtown streets have palms, low-rise shops, apartments and English storefront signs; Ocean Avenue faces lawns and the coast. Afternoon light is bright but often softened by marine haze, with cooler air near the water. Cyclists roll along the beach path while pedestrians, joggers and visitors cross the pier. Hear surf, gulls, bicycle bells and traffic. Casual shorts, light jackets and sunglasses are common; greetings include “Hey” and “How’s it going?”

The Las Vegas Strip is a wide desert boulevard edged by enormous hotel towers, themed façades, illuminated signs and elevated pedestrian bridges. At street level, cars inch past taxi stands while crowds move between casino entrances and shaded walkways. The Bellagio fountains send straight columns of water upward, then drop them back into the pool; their rush briefly rises above traffic and voices. Daylight is hard and dry, with pale mountains beyond the buildings; after dark, LEDs colour glass, stone and pavement. Most signs are in English. Visitors wear everything from T-shirts to evening clothes and greet one another with “Hi” or “Hey.”

San Francisco rises in steep blocks of narrow Victorian and Edwardian houses, bay windows, painted timber and closely parked cars. Downtown glass towers contrast with older brick buildings; English street signs mark intersections, and the Golden Gate Bridge appears across the water from suitable viewpoints. Fog can spill through the bridge towers and soften the afternoon light, though other neighbourhoods stay sunny. Buses and cars climb the grades slowly; cable cars run on a few central routes with a metallic bell and track rumble. Wind, gulls and traffic carry across the hills. People wear layers and often say “Hey” or “How’s it going?”

Miami Beach has broad white-sand beaches, turquoise shallows, palms and pastel Art Deco hotels, especially along Ocean Drive. Their rounded corners, horizontal bands and neon signs face outdoor café tables and slow-moving cars. Away from the beach, low apartment blocks and taller waterfront towers line flat streets with English and Spanish signs. Humid light is strong, afternoon clouds build quickly, and a short shower can leave glossy pavement. Hear surf, music from restaurants, bus engines and conversations over café dishes. Visitors wear swimwear with cover-ups; residents dress casually in the heat. Common greetings include “Hi,” “Hola” and “¿Qué tal?”

Chicago’s central skyline mixes dark steel-and-glass towers with pale stone and brick buildings beside the Chicago River. Elevated train tracks run between downtown façades, their trains clattering overhead as cars and pedestrians pass beneath. Eastward, Lake Michigan looks like a broad horizon of blue-grey water; wind can ruffle it into short waves. English signs mark streets, transit stops and shops. Summer brings bright light and waterfront walkers; winter light is low, with coats, scarves and sometimes snow piled at curbs. Hear train wheels, crossing bells, buses, wind and riverboat engines. On sidewalks, people commonly greet each other with “Hi” or “How are you?”

Washington’s National Mall is a long, open landscape of lawns, gravel paths and rows of trees, with the white Washington Monument rising near its centre. The US Capitol anchors the eastward view; the Lincoln Memorial sits beyond the Reflecting Pool to the west. Large stone museum buildings border the lawns, with English wayfinding signs and broad steps. Light falls across open grass with little shade at midday; summers are humid and winters can be bare and cold. Visitors walk, photograph landmarks and rest on benches while cyclists pass along the paths. Hear footsteps, birds, distant traffic and conversation. Greetings are usually “Hi” or “Hello.”

Houston spreads across flat ground in wide roads, overpasses, parking areas and neighbourhoods of brick houses, low shopping strips and trees. Downtown has a compact cluster of glass office towers; elsewhere, English and Spanish signs appear on businesses and roads. Summer air is hot and humid, sunlight reflects off car roofs, and thunderstorms can darken the sky and wet the asphalt within minutes. Cars dominate the movement, though people walk around parks, campuses and shopping districts. Hear traffic, air-conditioning units, insects in green areas and rain on pavement. Dress is generally casual and weather-conscious; greetings include “Hey,” “How y’all doing?” and “Howdy.”

Dearborn’s Arab commercial streets have low brick storefronts, bakeries, groceries and restaurants with Arabic and English lettering side by side. Along Warren Avenue, shop windows show bread trays, sweets and produce; nearby residential blocks have detached houses, lawns and parked cars. Mosques and community buildings appear among ordinary suburban streets, rather than defining every view. Summers are green and warm; winter brings bare trees, coats and sometimes snow along the curbs. Hear road traffic, shop doors, café conversation and occasional Arabic music indoors. Dress varies from jeans and work clothes to hijabs and modest coats. Neighbours may say “Hi,” “السلام عليكم” or “كيفك؟”

Toronto’s downtown mixes glass condo towers with older brick storefronts, with the CN Tower rising above the waterfront skyline. Wide streets have painted cycle lanes, streetcars running on rails, buses and frequent pedestrian crossings. English signs dominate, while many shops also display Chinese, Arabic or other languages. Summer light glints off Lake Ontario; winter brings low sun, slush and heavy coats. Streetcars hum and ring their bells, traffic hisses on wet pavement, and gulls call near the water. Commuters wear practical layers and carry backpacks or takeaway coffee. A casual greeting is “Hi” or “How’s it going?”

Vancouver has glass residential towers beside the water, with dark green mountains visible beyond the streets on clear days. Downtown blocks have broad crossings, bike lanes and English storefront signs; some neighbourhood shops also display Chinese characters. The SkyTrain glides on elevated tracks with a smooth electric whine, while buses brake and seaplanes buzz over the harbour. Rain often leaves pavement reflective under soft grey light, though summer afternoons can be bright and crisp. People wear rain jackets, trainers and backpacks, with cycling clothes common near the seawall. In cafés and on sidewalks, greetings are usually “Hi” or “How are you?”

Montreal’s streets mix pale stone buildings, brick apartment rows and exterior metal staircases with newer glass towers downtown. French dominates street signs and shop windows, sometimes alongside English. Mount Royal forms a low green backdrop, while the old port has cobbled stretches and masonry façades. Buses and cars roll past cyclists; below ground, Métro trains arrive with a rising electric sound. Summer café terraces glow in long evening light, while winter brings snowbanks, salt-streaked boots and thick parkas. People commonly say “Bonjour” on entering a shop, or “Salut” to someone they know. Church bells, conversation and traffic overlap on busy streets.

Mexico City spreads across a high basin: broad avenues, dense low-rise neighbourhoods, modern towers and the stone buildings around the Zócalo. Spanish lettering fills shopfronts, street stalls and road signs. Pink-and-white taxis, buses, motorcycles and pedestrians move through busy crossings; vendors push metal carts that rattle over paving. Daylight can be sharp in the dry season, with distant hills softened by haze, while summer afternoons often bring sudden rain. People dress in everyday urban clothes, from office wear to trainers and light jackets for cool mornings. Voices, horns and food-stall sizzles mix together. Common greetings include “Hola,” “Buenos días” and “¿Qué tal?”

Cancun’s hotel zone is a narrow strip of resorts between turquoise Caribbean water and the darker lagoon. White sand reflects strong sunlight; palms bend in sea breezes, and small waves hiss as they break. Hotel façades are pale concrete and glass, with Spanish and English signs at entrances. Inland, downtown streets have lower concrete buildings, shops, buses and Spanish storefront lettering. R1 and R2 buses rumble along Boulevard Kukulcán, mixed with taxis and tour vans. Visitors wear swimwear or light cotton near the beach; workers and residents wear uniforms or everyday clothes. Humid heat brings brief heavy showers. “Hola” and “Buenos días” are ordinary greetings.

Havana’s streets show pastel stucco walls, weathered balconies, arcades and taller apartment blocks beyond the older centre. Along the Malecón, a low seawall borders the road; wind pushes spray over it when the sea is rough. Spanish signs hang above shops and doorways. Older rounded cars share streets with newer vehicles, buses and pedestrians, their engines sounding different as they pass over uneven pavement. Bright tropical sun casts hard shadows, while humid air softens the distance. People wear light shirts, dresses and sandals, often pausing to talk in doorways. Conversations, traffic and occasional music carry between buildings. Greetings include “Hola” and “¿Qué tal?”

Copacabana curves around a broad sandy beach backed by closely packed apartment and hotel towers. Its seaside promenade has unmistakable black-and-white wave-pattern stone paving, with a busy road running alongside. Portuguese signs appear on shops, kiosks and beach-service stands. Atlantic waves break in white bands; vendors call out, cyclists pass, and traffic forms a steady low roar. Bright sun makes the sand glare, while humid, cloudy days flatten the colours and rain darkens the paving. Beachgoers wear swimwear and flip-flops; on the inland streets, people wear light casual clothes. Common greetings are “Oi,” “Bom dia” and “Tudo bem?”

São Paulo has a dense skyline of concrete and glass towers stretching far beyond the centre. Avenida Paulista is a wide corridor of office buildings, shops, buses and crowds; the red supports of MASP lift its main building above an open space. Portuguese signs fill storefronts and traffic directions. Cars, motorcycles and buses stream through broad junctions, with engines, horns and bus brakes audible above conversation. Daylight is often bright but softened by haze; warm-season downpours quickly turn gutters into rushing channels. Commuters wear office clothes, jeans or trainers and carry bags against sudden rain. People greet each other with “Oi,” “Bom dia” or “Tudo bem?”

Broad avenues lined with plane trees run past cream stone façades, ornate balconies and mid-rise apartment blocks. The white Obelisk rises above Avenida 9 de Julio; older streets near Plaza de Mayo have domes and ironwork. Black-and-yellow taxis, buses called colectivos and motorcycles move through busy intersections, with engines, horns and conversations audible at crossings. Shop signs are in Spanish. Summer sun is strong and humid; winter light is lower and cooler, with fallen leaves along the pavements. Commuters wear casual or office clothes, and people commonly greet each other with “hola,” “buen día” or “¿cómo andás?”

Lima spreads across a dry coastal plain, with dense low-rise neighbourhoods, unfinished brick walls and newer glass towers around Miraflores and San Isidro. The Miraflores cliffs drop toward the Pacific, where surf breaks below parks and roads. Downtown has carved balconies and pale historic façades. Signs are mostly Spanish. Buses, taxis and motorcycles fill the roads; engines and frequent horns mix with vendors’ calls and the sound of waves near the coast. Winter often brings a flat grey marine mist called garúa, while summer is brighter and warm. People wear everyday casual or office clothes and greet others with “buenos días” or “¿qué tal?”

Nairobi’s centre mixes concrete office blocks and glass towers with street trees, while outlying roads pass markets, apartment buildings and walled compounds. Some avenues turn purple when jacarandas bloom. Signs commonly use English and Swahili. Colourfully painted matatus stop and pull into traffic alongside cars, buses and boda boda motorcycles; expect engine noise, horns, music from vehicles and street conversations. Daylight is often bright at this high elevation, with cooler mornings and evenings and heavy showers in rainy periods. People wear anything from office shirts and suits to casual clothes. Familiar greetings include “habari?” and “sasa?”, often answered with “poa.”

Flat-topped Table Mountain stands behind Cape Town, with Lion’s Head beside it and the harbour facing the sea. Central streets mix glass offices, older plastered buildings and cafés; Bo-Kaap has tightly packed houses painted vivid pink, blue and green. Signs appear in English, Afrikaans and isiXhosa. Cars, buses and minibus taxis travel beneath the mountain, accompanied by traffic noise, wind and seabirds near the waterfront. Summer light is sharp and often windy; winter can be cool, cloudy and rainy. Clothing ranges from office wear to light casual layers. Depending on language and company, greetings include “howzit,” “molo” and “hoe gaan dit?”

Johannesburg sits inland on rolling high ground, not beside the sea. Its centre has older stone buildings and tall concrete towers; Sandton has reflective glass high-rises, while residential areas mix brick houses, walls, trees and apartment blocks. Pale mine dumps are visible from some roads. Signs appear in English and several local languages. Minibus taxis, buses and cars crowd major routes; engines, horns, taxi-rank calls and conversations shape the street sound. Winter brings dry air, yellow grass and crisp sunshine; summer brings green trees and afternoon thunderstorms. People wear varied casual and business clothes, greeting each other with “howzit,” “sawubona” or “dumela,” depending on language.

Lagos stretches around lagoons and bridges. Glass towers and offices rise on Victoria Island, while many mainland streets are lined with concrete shops, painted walls, market stalls and dense housing. English signage sits alongside Yoruba names and locally worded advertisements. Yellow danfo minibuses, cars, motorcycles and pedestrians negotiate heavy traffic; horns, conductors calling destinations, music and market voices overlap. Humid light can turn hazy, and tropical downpours leave roads shining before the sun returns. Office workers, traders and students wear varied Western and traditional clothing. Common greetings include “good morning,” Nigerian Pidgin “how far?” and, among Yoruba speakers, “ẹ káàárọ̀.”

Accra has low- and mid-rise concrete buildings, busy roadside shops and newer glass offices, with Atlantic surf along parts of the coast. The Independence Arch is a pale landmark near broad roads; older Jamestown streets have weathered façades and fishing activity. Signs are largely in English, often beside brightly coloured advertisements. Tro-tro minibuses stop for passengers among taxis and cars, creating a mix of horns, conductors’ calls, conversation and coastal wind. Sunlight is strong and humid; rainy periods bring sudden heavy showers. People wear office clothes, casual outfits or patterned fabrics according to the occasion. Greetings include “good morning” and, in Twi, “ɛte sɛn?”

Addis Ababa climbs across highland slopes, mixing new glass-and-concrete buildings with older plastered shops, corrugated roofs and eucalyptus-lined roads. Meskel Square opens into a broad paved gathering space, and light-rail tracks cross parts of the city. Signs are primarily in Amharic script, often with English. Blue-and-white minibuses, cars and pedestrians fill junctions; engines, horns, conductors calling routes and café conversations carry through the streets. The elevation makes mornings and evenings cool even under bright sun, and rain can fall hard in the wet season. Dress ranges from office wear to casual clothes and white netela shawls near churches. People greet one another with “selam” and “dehna neh?” or “dehna nesh?”

Stone Town is a dense maze of narrow, uneven lanes between pale coral-stone buildings coated in weathered lime plaster. Shaded balconies project above carved wooden doors, some fitted with brass studs. Small shops display signs in Swahili and English; pedestrians step aside for bicycles and handcarts. At the seafront, Forodhani Gardens opens onto the water, with fishing boats rocking gently offshore. Humid light softens cream walls by day and turns warm at sunset. Expect footsteps on stone, bicycle bells, conversation and calls to prayer. People wear everything from light shirts to kanzu and headscarves; a common greeting is “Habari?”

Marrakech medina is packed with red-ochre plaster walls, tall blank facades, arched passages and shopfronts crowded with leather goods, metal lanterns and textiles. Its lanes alternate between bright sun and deep shade; scooters thread slowly past walkers, handcarts and occasional donkeys. Near Jemaa el-Fnaa, the square opens wide beneath the visible Koutoubia minaret. Dry air and dusty afternoon light make the pink-brown buildings glow. Listen for scooter engines, bargaining voices, cart wheels and the call to prayer. Locals wear both contemporary clothes and djellabas. Greetings include “Salam alaykum” and the Moroccan Arabic “Labas?”

Dakar stretches across a coastal peninsula, mixing concrete apartment blocks, glass office towers in the Plateau district and low-rise streets painted in bright, fading colours. The Atlantic is visible from seafront roads; the African Renaissance Monument stands high above the city on the Mamelles hills. Yellow-and-black taxis, buses and decorated car rapides jostle through traffic, while vendors walk between stopped vehicles. Sunlight is strong, sometimes softened by sea mist or dusty Harmattan haze. Hear horns, engines, street conversation and surf near the shore. Clothing ranges from T-shirts and jeans to colourful boubous. In Wolof, people greet one another with “Nanga def?”

Kigali spreads over steep green hills, with clusters of terracotta and metal roofs below modern glass-fronted buildings in the centre. Paved roads curve around the slopes; motorcycle taxis lean into bends, their drivers and passengers wearing helmets. Roadside shops and billboards carry Kinyarwanda and English, sometimes French. Clear morning light reveals distant ridgelines, while rain can darken the asphalt and make leafy verges shine. Expect motorcycle engines, birds, conversations and traffic rather than a continuous roar. People wear contemporary office clothes, casual wear and patterned fabrics. A Kinyarwanda greeting is “Muraho”; friends may ask “Amakuru?” and answer “Ni meza.”
